newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries slip in a torpor in summer trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries slip in a torpor in summer trade.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended flat to slightly higher in a market mired in the apathy of a sweltering summer session.

Treasuries had been pressured at the open by a somewhat stronger-than-expected U.S. June retail sales report. But the market soon recouped its losses on a second look at the report and another set of retail data which was weak.
"There is nothing like building up anticipation about an economic report for two weeks. And then nothing happens," noted HSBC Markets senior economist Christopher Low.

"We have never seen a report so close to consensus that it left the market essentially speechless," Low said of the June U.S. retail sales reported up 0.5 percent versus expectations for a 0.2-percent rise. "This report was as void of new information as is possible."
The larger-than-forecast gain was offset by a downward revision of the May decline, first reported at down 0.1 percent, to down 0.3 percent.
The retail sales report confirmed that the demand side of the U.S. economy cooled off through most of the second quarter and then picked up some toward the end.
The American consumer remains the key factor of uncertainty weighing on the U.S. growth and interest rate outlook in the second half of 1997.
The Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Redbook weekly survey gave some hint of moderate consumer demand as its retail sales index slipped 0.2 percent in the week ended July 12.
"The number was weak. But the report said sales were on par or above plans. Retailers were pleased," Low said of the full Redbook report, available to subscribers only.
Traders said the market has fully priced in all the best news about growth and inflation.
They said it would take a "shocker" to force the 30-year bond yield out of a 6.50 percent-to-6-7/8 percent range.

"The problem is that we have become very complacent about good growth and low inflation," Low remarked. "We've gotten to the point where the Consumer Price Index (CPI) could be down tomorrow and that would even not raise an eyebrow."
A Reuters poll sees CPI and core CPI at 0.2 percent versus up 0.1 percent and up 0.2 percent, respectively, in May.
The other main U.S. economic report on Wednesday is June industrial production, seen up 0.2 percent, and capacity utilization, seen at 83.6 percent versus May's 83.7 percent.
Traders said the Dow Jones industrial average and the dollar, both at lofty levels, may play an unusually important role for Treasuries at this juncture.

Foreign funds, mainly from Europe, have contributed to the bond rally to 6.50 percent. A reversal of fortune for dollar/mark, talked down by Bundesbank officials in the afternoon, could trigger capital repatriation.
But Treasuries could draw strength from a move out of equities and into debt if investors find the Dow -- which closed a mere 25 points from the stratospheric 8000 barrier -- ripe for profit-taking.
In late trading, the 30-year bond was up 3/32 at 101-00/32 to yield 6.55 percent.
The two-year note was unchanged at 100-4/32 to yield 5.93 percent, so was the five-year at 100-12/32 and 6.16 percent. The 10-year note ended off 1/32 at 102-21/32 and 6.26 percent.
Also, the three- and six-month and one-year bills were flat at rates of 5.06, 5.11 and 5.24 percent.
